sections.title_en: Preface: Why I Write This Book
en: I have called my art of strategy the Niten Ichi school, and after several years of training in it, I now intend to set it down in writing for the first time.

It is now early in the tenth month of the twentieth year of Kan’ei (1643). I climbed Iwato Mountain in Higo province in Kyushu, faced the heavens and offered my prayers, paid honor to Kannon, and before the image of the Buddha I declared myself: I am Shinmen Musashi Fujiwara no Genshin, a warrior from Harima province, now about sixty years old. From my youth my heart has been set on the path of strategy. At thirteen I fought my first duel, defeating the strategist Arima Kihei of the Shintō school. At sixteen I defeated Akiyama, a powerful strategist from Tajima province. At twenty-one I made my way to the capital, where I met strategists from across the realm and decided several contests, never failing to win any of them. After that I traveled from province to province, meeting strategists of many schools, and fought more than sixty contests without once losing an advantage. All of this took place from my thirteenth year into my late twenties.

When I passed thirty and looked back, I saw that my victories had not come from fully mastering strategy. Perhaps it was a natural aptitude that never strayed from heaven’s principle, or perhaps the other schools were simply weak. Still, I wanted to reach deeper principles, so I trained morning and evening, and around the age of fifty I came to grasp the true principle of strategy. From then on I had no further road to search, and I have simply passed my days since.

Applying the benefits of strategy to the paths of all the arts and skills, I have no master in any matter. In writing this book I have not drawn on the sayings of Buddhism or Confucianism, nor on old war chronicles or military manuals. I set down the real spirit of this single school, using heaven’s principle and Kannon as my mirror. I took up my brush on the tenth night of the tenth month, in the early part of the hour of the tiger, and began to write.
sections.gist: Musashi, now about sixty, recounts his duels from age thirteen and says he is writing down his school’s principles for the first time.
sections.lesson: Early wins can hide what you have not really learned. Look back honestly at how you succeeded, and separate skill from luck before you pass your methods on to others.

terms.en: strategy, the martial art and its law
Mount Iwato in Higo, where Musashi prayed

en: Strategy is the law of the warrior. Commanders in particular must practice this law, and even ordinary soldiers must understand its Way. Today there is no samurai in the world who truly grasps the path of strategy. Consider the ways people do follow: the Buddhist Way of saving others, the Confucian study of letters, the physician’s art of curing every illness, the poet’s study of waka, the tea masters, archers, connoisseurs, and all the other arts and accomplishments. Each person practices whatever appeals to him, according to his own heart. Very few people take up the path of strategy.

Warriors speak of the twofold path of letters and arms, and they should cultivate both. Even if a man is clumsy in this Way, every warrior should practice strategy to the degree his station allows. If I measure what most warriors think, they seem to cultivate nothing more than the way of dying. Yet readiness to die is not limited to warriors: monks, women, farmers and people of lower rank can know duty, feel shame and resolve to die when it is needed, and in that there is no difference. What distinguishes the warrior’s practice of strategy is that in everything he aims for the highest excellence. He wins a duel with one man or a battle against many, serving his lord and his own name and raising himself in the world. Such is the merit that strategy brings.

Still, some people think that even if they study strategy it will be of no use in a real moment. For them, the answer is to practice so that it can be used at any time, and to teach everything so that it is useful in every matter. That is the real path of strategy.
sections.gist: Musashi says few people truly understand strategy, the warrior’s law, and that most people choose arts for taste, so few take up the martial path seriously.
sections.lesson: Many people dabble in several pursuits without depth. Choose the work that matters for your role and train in it seriously, instead of collecting interests that only look impressive.

terms.en: the warrior house, the samurai class
the twofold path of letters and arms

en: Even in China and in our own land, those who practiced this path were handed down as masters of strategy. There should be no warrior who does not study this law.

In recent times, people who make a living as ‘strategists’ are really just swordsmen. The attendants of the Kashima and Kantori shrines in Hitachi province claimed to have received the teaching from the gods; they founded schools and traveled from land to land teaching people. That is the recent use of the word. In older times the martial craft was counted among the ten abilities and seven accomplishments, valued for practical use. It is indeed an art, but once it is treated as a practical benefit, it cannot be limited to sword technique alone. If you understand only one slice of swordsmanship, you will not even know the sword well, and it certainly will not meet the law of war.

Looking at the world, people turn every art into merchandise. They make themselves into goods for sale and dress up their tools to sell as well. Flower and fruit are two aspects of the same thing, and there is less fruit than blossom. Above all, in the art of strategy people add color and try to make it bloom, showing off their techniques. Some open one dojo, some two, and teach the art, hoping to profit from it. Who would not call this a flashy, hollow display? It is surely the root of great harm. Someone once said that immature strategy is the root of great calamity, and it was a true saying.

People make their way through life along four paths: those of the farmer, the merchant, the warrior and the craftsman. The farmer keeps many kinds of tools and, watching the turning seasons, spends spring and autumn without a moment to rest. That is the farmer’s path. The merchant, such as a brewer, gathers the materials he needs, judges their quality and uses them, and makes his living from his own labor and profit. Every trade works this way, and that is the merchant’s path. The warrior should prepare many kinds of weapons and understand each one’s strengths. A warrior who does not practice with his weapons or know their uses is a shallow sort of warrior. The craftsman uses a range of tools, skillfully makes and uses each one, keeps his ink line and measures, and gets through life working with his hands. These are the four paths.

I describe the art of strategy by comparing it to carpentry. The comparison works through the idea of the house: the houses of court nobles and warriors, the rise or fall of a family house, the style and traditions of a house, its name. That is why I borrow from carpentry. The character for carpenter, 大工, can also be read as ‘great craft’, and strategy is a great craft, so I write about it through the image of the carpenter.
If you want to learn this art, study this book. The teacher is like the needle and the student like the thread: each must be bound to the other, and you must keep practicing without pause.
sections.gist: Strategy is more than swordsmanship. Sword technique alone does not reach the law of war, and showy display for profit corrupts the art.
sections.lesson: Be wary of looking skilled through showmanship or branding. Real competence is what helps when it counts, and advertising yourself as an expert does not replace it.

terms.en: the ten abilities and seven accomplishments

en: The commander is like the head carpenter. He must know the standards of the realm, measure the standards of his province, and understand the standards of his own house; this is the head’s way. The head carpenter must know the design of temples, halls, pagodas and mansions, direct his people, and raise up houses. A head carpenter and a warrior commander are the same in this. In building a house, the timber is chosen with care. Straight, knot-free wood of good appearance goes into the visible pillars, and straight wood with a few knots but good strength goes into the inner pillars. Fine-looking timber, though slightly weak, serves for sills, crossbeams, doors and sliding screens if it has no knots. Strong timber that is gnarled or warped can be used with judgment, and a house built with careful choices will not easily fall apart for a long time. Timber that is weak and full of knots should be used for scaffolding, or in the end for firewood.

When the commander assigns carpenters, he must know their grade: upper, middle or lower. Some are sent to the corners and the joinery, others to sliding doors, sills, lintels, ceilings and the rest, each according to his skill. The weaker ones are made to lay the floor joists, and the weakest are made to carve wedges. If he judges his people well and assigns them accordingly, the work progresses quickly and the results are skillful. What is praised is an effective, capable job, and one should allow no shortcoming in anything. Knowing the spirit of upper, middle and lower men is how a commander encourages them, and knowing what is unreasonable is how he restrains them. These matters all lie in the commander’s mind.
Such are the benefits of strategy.
sections.gist: A commander, like a head carpenter, must know his materials and his people, matching each person and each piece of timber to the task that suits its strength.
sections.lesson: When you lead a team, assign work by each person’s real strengths and limits. Put flawed or weak resources to uses they can handle, rather than forcing them into critical roles.

terms.en: head, leader; the foreman or commander

en: A trooper must be like a carpenter, grinding his own blades by his own hands and making all kinds of assault implements. He keeps them in a carpenter’s box and takes on the work the commander assigns. He cuts columns and beams with an adze, planes floorboards and shelves smooth, cuts and carves tight joinery and decoration, and polishes the surfaces, finishing every corner and every detail with skill. This is the carpenter’s craft. Once a man has practiced this work and learned it well, and understands the standards thoroughly, he can become the commander. A carpenter’s discipline is to keep his tools well sharpened and in good condition. From tall cabinets, bookshelves, desks and tables to lamp stands, cutting boards and pot lids, he makes everything with mastery. The trooper should be like this, and he should examine it carefully.
The carpenter’s discipline is this: do not let the wood warp, keep the joints aligned, plane well, do not over-polish, and do not let the work split later. These are essential.
Anyone who wishes to learn this art should give full attention to each matter written in this book and weigh it carefully.
sections.gist: Ordinary troopers must master their tools and craft from the bottom up, learning by doing, so that they can later be trusted to lead.
sections.lesson: Keep your tools sharp and learn the basics of your job thoroughly. Competence built through hands-on work is what earns responsibility later.

sections.title_en: Why the Book Has Five Scrolls
en: I divide the Way into five parts and write each in its own scroll so that its benefit can be known: Earth, Water, Fire, Wind and Void.

The Earth scroll sets out the overall structure of the Way of strategy as seen in my school. Mere sword technique cannot reach the true Way. One must know the smallest and the largest matters, the shallowest and the deepest, and go from the simple to the profound, like laying out a straight road over level ground. That is why the first scroll is called Earth: it levels the ground.

The Water scroll: the mind takes on the nature of water. Water takes the shape of whatever holds it, becoming a single drop in a small vessel or a vast sea in a large one, and it can show a clear blue depth. The clear part is what I use to show the principles of my school in this scroll.

When you clearly understand the principle of sword technique and can freely defeat a single opponent, you are in effect defeating everyone. The mind that defeats one enemy is the same as the mind that defeats a thousand. A commander’s strategy is to make the small into the large, as one builds a full-size Buddha statue from a model only one foot tall. The details cannot be fully written here. Mastering one thing lets you know thousands, which is the benefit of strategy. This principle is written out in the Water scroll.

The Fire scroll is about fighting. Fire is fierce whether it is small or great, and battles are the same. The principle of combat is the same for a duel between two men and a battle of ten thousand a side. Understand that the spirit can be large or small. Large things are easy to see; small things are hard to see. A large body of men is slow to shift position, so its movements can be predicted; an individual can change his mind in an instant, so his movements are hard to predict. You must understand this. The core of this scroll lies in drilling without pause, so that decisions come quickly. In strategy, training must be part of ordinary life, with the spirit unchanged. That is why the fighting of war is set out in this scroll.

Because matters of fire happen in the blink of an eye, you must become so familiar with them that you practice them daily as routine, with an unchanged mind; this is the essence of strategy. For that reason, I set out the matters of victory and defeat in battle in the Fire scroll.

The Wind scroll is not about my own school. It describes the strategies of other schools and their practices. ‘Wind’ refers to the old traditions and the present-day ones, and to the traditions of each family and each school. Understanding others is necessary before one can understand oneself. Every Way has side paths. If you practice a Way daily but your spirit wanders, you may believe you are on a good path while, viewed objectively, it is not the true one. When one walks the genuine path and strays only slightly, the error grows large later. Keep this in mind.

People naturally assume strategy is only sword fighting, and that is understandable. My strategy, however, has its own separate principle beyond the sword. So that people can understand the strategy of the world, I describe other schools in the Wind scroll.

The Void scroll: the Void has neither a fixed start nor a fixed end. Once one begins to talk about it, one cannot say what is inside or outside, what is deep or shallow. When you grasp the principle, you step beyond principles. In the art of strategy you find freedom within yourself and a remarkable power of your own, and at the right moment you read the rhythm and strike the enemy and yourself naturally. All of this is the Void. The Void scroll records how one enters the true path naturally.
sections.gist: The book has five scrolls, moving from the basic structure of Musashi’s school to fighting, to rival schools, and finally to the formless Void.
sections.lesson: Structure a hard subject as a progression, from fundamentals to application to context, so learners can build understanding step by step.

terms.en: Earth, Water, Fire, Wind and Void: the five scrolls
the Wind scroll, on other schools

sections.title_en: Why Two Swords: The Niten Ichi School
en: Now the matter of the two swords. Warriors, whether commanders or troopers, carry two blades at the belt. Long ago they went by the names tachi and katana; today we say sword and short sword. Enough said: in our country, for whatever reason, samurai wear two blades at the waist. That is the warrior’s Way. This school is named Niten Ichi-ryū to show the benefits of using both swords. Spears and halberds are carried outdoors and belong to a different category of weapon, so they are counted among the battle equipment.

In this school, a beginner should first train with the long sword and the sword, one in each hand. This is the real method. When you give up your life, use every tool you have; it is not what you want, to die with your weapons still unused at your waist. Yet holding something in each hand does not allow free movement to either side. So the purpose of training with a sword in each hand is to learn to take up the long sword in one hand.

Spears, long halberds and other large weapons are in a separate class. A short sword and a sword can each be held in one hand. Holding the long sword with both hands is a fault: on horseback, on rough roads, on swampy ground, in muddy paddies, on rocky ground and in a crowd, it is awkward. Holding a bow, spear or other weapon in the left hand leaves only the right hand free for the long sword. Since nearly every weapon is used with one hand, using both hands for the long sword is not the true practice. If you cannot cut down an enemy with one hand, use both, which takes no extra effort.

First, to learn to swing a sword with one hand, this school trains with two. When a sword is first picked up, it feels heavy and hard to swing; a bow is hard to draw and a halberd hard to wield. But with use, the bow’s pull grows stronger, and once the sword is swung often, you gain the power of the Way and it swings well. The principle of the long sword is not to swing fast; it is explained in the Water scroll. The long sword is swung in open space, the short sword in narrow space: this is the basic meaning of the practice.

In this school you can win with a long blade and you can win with a short one, so the length of the sword is not fixed. Long or short, this school wins with whichever blade is used. The heart that can win with whatever is at hand is the Way of this school. Carrying two swords is better than carrying one when you must fight many men alone, or when you need to dislodge someone barricaded inside a building.
Such matters need not be spelled out here. Grasp one principle and its variations will be plain to you; practice the Way and nothing will seem hidden. Think carefully about this.
sections.gist: Warriors carry two swords. Training with one in each hand builds one-handed control and flexibility, and the sword must be usable in every situation.
sections.lesson: Deliberately practice your weaker side or a less natural method. Limiting yourself to one way of working leaves you unprepared when conditions change.

sections.title_en: Understanding the Two Characters of Strategy
en: Those who have mastered the sword in this art are called strategists in the world. In the other martial arts, one who masters the bow is called an archer, one who masters the gun is a gunner, one who masters the spear is a spearman, and one who masters the halberd is a halberd man. But one who masters the sword is not called a long-swordsman or a companion-swordsman. The bow, the gun, the spear and the halberd are all warriors’ equipment, so they are also part of strategy. Still, it is reasonable to name the whole art after the sword.

Because the sword is the core of the Way, one who gains the sword’s virtue can govern the world and himself, and so the long sword is the foundation of strategy. Its principle is ‘strategy through the long sword’. Someone who gains the virtue of the sword can overcome ten. A hundred can then overcome a thousand, and a thousand can overcome ten thousand. In my strategy, one and ten thousand are treated alike, so this is the complete craft of the warrior.

Confucian scholars, Buddhist monks, tea connoisseurs, etiquette teachers and dancers are not part of the warrior’s Way. Even though those paths lie outside the warrior’s Way, if one knows the Way widely one meets it everywhere. Each person should polish his own Way with care.
sections.gist: One who masters the sword is known as a strategist, since the sword underlies the martial arts, and a truly trained man can in principle face many opponents.
sections.lesson: Identify the core skill that makes everything else work and develop it deeply. Mastering the foundation gives you leverage across related tasks.

terms.en: a master of the long sword

sections.title_en: Knowing the Benefit of Each Weapon
en: Learn the usefulness of each weapon. Whichever one you carry will come up depending on the occasion. The short sword is best in a cramped spot, close to the enemy’s body. The long sword is useful almost anywhere, since it fits many situations. On the battlefield the halberd falls behind the spear: the spear takes the lead while the halberd follows. Among men of equal training the spear has a slight edge, and in tight spaces the spear and halberd both lose much of their use. Neither works well against a man barricaded in a building, so they are mainly weapons for the field. Still, battlefield weapons are essential in war. But if you cling to the advantages of indoor practice and forget the authentic path, you will find yourself unprepared in a real encounter.

In field battles the bow is useful for maneuvering and for drawing the enemy out, and it works well when spears and other arms engage at close range. For storming a castle, or when the enemy is twenty ken away, roughly forty paces, it is inadequate. For this reason, few archery schools are kept alive today, and the skill sees little use. In the present age, arts that are rich in show but poor in substance do not serve in critical moments. The gun is unmatched inside a fortress. Before the lines clash on open ground it has its uses, but once the fighting begins it is inadequate. The virtue of the bow is that the arrow in flight can be seen, while a bullet cannot be. This must be carefully considered.
A horse must be sturdy, responsive and free of vices. This is essential.

For all weapons: the horse should be large and strong, the sword and short sword should cut broadly, the spear and long halberd should thrust through, and bows and guns should be sturdy and not easily damaged. Do not favor any small detail in your equipment, for excess is no better than lack. Do not merely imitate others; fit your weapons to your own body so that they suit your hand.
Commanders and troopers alike who favor some things and dislike others are in error. Cultivating even-handed judgment is essential.
sections.gist: Each weapon suits different settings: swords for tight spaces, spears and halberds for open fields, bows and guns for set ranges. Choose tools that fit you.
sections.lesson: Choose tools and methods by context, and make sure your equipment fits your own body and habits instead of copying what others use. Do not train only for artificial settings.

en: Everything has its rhythm, but the rhythm of strategy is hard to reach without training. The rhythm of the world shows itself in the arts: dance, ceremonial performance, pipes and strings, all of which keep a good and steady pace. Across the martial arts, including archery, gunnery, horsemanship and every other skill, rhythm is present, and you must never go against it. Even in empty matters there is rhythm. A warrior’s life has rhythms for rising in service, rhythms for falling back, rhythms that fit and rhythms that clash. A merchant’s fortune likewise has rhythms of gain and loss, and each path has its own. Look carefully at the rhythms of growth and decline in things.

Strategy involves many rhythms. First, know the rhythms that meet and the rhythms that clash. Within the rhythms, know the large and the small, the fast and the slow; know the rhythm that strikes, the rhythm of the interval, and the rhythm that works against you. This knowledge is the core of strategy. If you do not learn to recognize the rhythm that works against you, your strategy will be unreliable. In battle, study the rhythm of each enemy and strike with a timing he does not anticipate; draw the rhythm of the Void from the rhythm of wisdom, and win. Every scroll is chiefly concerned with rhythm, so study the principles written in them and train diligently.

By practicing this one school of strategy morning after morning and evening after evening, the heart naturally broadens. So I now write down, for the first time, what I have passed on to the world as one portion of strategy: these five scrolls of Earth, Water, Fire, Wind and Void.

Those who want to learn my strategy should follow these principles: first, harbor no crooked thoughts; second, drill in the Way itself; third, become acquainted with the other arts; fourth, know the Way of each trade; fifth, discern gain and loss in every matter; sixth, learn to judge things with a keen eye; seventh, perceive what cannot be seen and understand it; eighth, pay attention even to small things; ninth, do nothing that serves no purpose. Hold these broad principles in your mind and train in the Way of strategy accordingly. Whoever looks at matters only narrowly will find it hard to master strategy. A practitioner who learns this method need not fear twenty or thirty opponents. First keep up your strategy without pause and follow the straight Way: with your hands you will win, and with your eyes you will beat others. Through training you gain complete freedom, so your body can overcome others; and with familiarity in the Way, your mind can overcome others. Once you reach this point, how could you be defeated? In the broader strategy of a leader, good people serve better than great numbers; he directs troops well, corrects his own conduct, governs the land, nourishes the people and follows the laws of the age. In every Way, knowing where you cannot be defeated helps you and preserves your name. This is the Way of strategy. Shōhō 2 (1645), fifth month, twelfth day: Shinmen Musashi, to Terao Magonojō. Kanbun 7 (1667), second month, fifth day: Terao Musei Katsunobu, with his monogram, to Yamamoto Gensuke.
sections.gist: Every skill has a rhythm. Strategy means reading both sides’ rhythm and striking when the enemy does not expect it; the five scrolls are about timing.
sections.lesson: In meetings or negotiations, watch the rhythm of the room and time your moves when others are not ready. Good timing often matters more than force.

en: Because the Niten Ichi school builds on the spirit of water and teaches the principles of gaining advantage, this is the Water Book, in which I write out the sword lines of our school. This Way cannot be spelled out in full detail, and however carefully I put it into words, the words will fall short; still, the advantage will make itself heard. Take every point written here one character at a time and think it through. If you read it in broad strokes you will often go astray. Even when a passage speaks of a duel between one man and another, understand it as applying to a battle of ten thousand against ten thousand, and weigh that well. In this Way above all, if you mistake the path even slightly, you become confused and fall onto the bad road. Do not read these notes as if they were about someone else, do not think of them as rote lessons to memorize, and do not treat them as imitations. Instead, find the advantage from your own heart and keep working at it, placing yourself fully inside the situation.
sections.gist: Musashi introduces the Water Book: the principles of advantage must be understood deeply and drawn from one's own heart, not learned from written words alone.
sections.lesson: Read a principle, then test it against your own work and situation rather than memorizing it. Ask what the lesson means for the decision you face today.

en: In the principles of strategy, your state of mind must not be different from your everyday mind. Keep the mind open and direct, neither stiffly drawn tight nor slack in the least, and not leaning to any side. Set it in the center, calm yet never stagnant, and examine closely that it never wavers, even for an instant. A still moment does not mean the mind is still, and a hurried moment does not mean the mind is hurried. The mind should not follow the body, and the body should not follow the mind. Be watchful with your mind while your body does not look as if it is on guard. Leave no lapse in the mind and let nothing slip even a little. Even if the outer mind seems weak, keep the inner mind firm and do not let others see into it. A person of small stature must know the great matters fully in the mind, and a person of large stature must know the small matters well. Whether large or small, keep the mind straight and do not play favorites with your own body. Keep the inner mind clear and wide, and place your wisdom in that open space. Polish mind and wisdom together until both are sharp. Know right and wrong in the world, know good and evil in all things, and pass through the many arts, each by its own path, so that no one can fool you. Then that wisdom becomes the wisdom of strategy. In the wisdom of strategy there is one common mistake to avoid. Even on the battlefield, when everything is hurried, keep working at the principles of strategy until your mind is unshaken.
sections.gist: Keep the mind calm, open and unbiased, neither tense nor slack, in both daily life and combat, and polish wisdom by learning across many arts.
sections.lesson: Before a high-stakes meeting or deadline, steady your breathing, stay open to other views, and avoid tunnel vision. A calm, wide attention lets you see the next move clearly.

en: Hold your bearing like this: do not droop the head, do not tilt it up, do not lean it to one side, and do not let it twist. Keep the brow smooth and the space between the eyebrows free of creases. Let the eyeballs stay still and do not blink; narrow the eyes slightly so that the face looks calm and composed. Keep the line of the nose straight with a slight sense of the chin pushed forward. Keep the back of the neck straight and put a little strength into the nape, so that the whole body feels even from the shoulders down. Drop both shoulders, straighten the back, and do not stick out the buttocks. Put strength into the legs, down to the toes, and keep the waist from bending. It is taught to wedge the belly: press the belly against the short sword in its scabbard so that the sash does not loosen, as if setting a wedge. In general, in strategy, make your everyday body your fighting body, and make your fighting body your everyday body. Study this carefully.
sections.gist: Set the body upright and relaxed: level head, steady eyes, dropped shoulders, strong legs and a braced belly, so everyday and fighting posture match.
sections.lesson: Carry the same composed bearing into ordinary work that you would use under pressure. A steady posture signals calm to colleagues and keeps you alert in routine meetings.

en: Keep your eyes wide and open in how you look. There are two ways of seeing, kan and ken: kan is perceiving the whole, and ken is seeing the particulars. The kan should be firm; the ken should be light. Perceive far things as though they were at hand, and near things as though they were distant. Strategy demands that you recognize the enemy's blade while barely glancing at it. This is the great secret of strategy; work it out for yourself.

This way of placing the eyes is the same whether the martial art is small or large. Keep the eyeballs still while you take in both sides; this is essential. In a hurry you will not grasp it at once. Memorize these notes, keep this way of looking at all times, and study carefully so that your eye placement never changes, no matter what happens.
sections.gist: Look broadly: take in the whole with a firm perception while watching details lightly, and know the enemy's sword without fixating on its movement.
sections.lesson: In meetings, keep the big picture and the room in view while still catching the one detail that matters. Fixating on a single worry blinds you to everything else.

terms.en: perceiving the whole and seeing the detail

en: Hold the long sword with the thumb and forefinger as if they float, the middle finger neither clenched nor limp, and the last two fingers held snugly shut. It is bad to have any slack in the hands. When you take up the sword, feel that you are going to cut the enemy. Do not change your grip as you cut, and do not let your hands cringe. When you bat aside the enemy's blade, ward it off, press it down, or receive it, change the feel of the thumb and forefinger only slightly; above all, be resolved to cut the enemy with the way you hold the sword. The grip for a practice cut on test targets and the grip for cutting a man are the same.
In general, with the sword or with the hands, dislike being fixed in place. A stuck hand is a dead hand; a hand that stays free is a living hand. Understand this well.
sections.gist: Hold the sword with a relaxed but firm grip, never letting the hands stiffen or go slack, and always intend to cut through on contact.
sections.lesson: Hold your tools, plans and commitments firmly but without rigidity. Keep your grip loose enough to adjust when conditions change.

terms.en: the grip, the hands on the sword

en: Let the toes float a little and press down firmly with the heels. Move quickly or slowly, in long or short steps; your feet should always travel as they do in ordinary walking. Three kinds of footwork are disliked in this Way: the jumping foot, the floating foot, and the stuck foot that stamps and stops. The great principle of this Way is called yin-yang footing, and it is essential. Yin-yang footing means never moving just one foot. Whether you are cutting, pulling back, or receiving a blow, step right and left in turn. Never let one foot do all the stepping. Examine this again and again.
sections.gist: Keep the feet moving as in normal walking, heels pressing, and alternate both feet; never let one foot carry the movement alone.
sections.lesson: Keep steady, balanced progress across your projects rather than relying on one big push. Spread the load so no single part of your work carries everything.

en: The five stances are these: upper, middle, lower, a right-side stance and a left-side stance. Although I divide the stances into five, all of them are for cutting the enemy, and there are no stances beyond these five. Whichever stance you assume, do not think that you are making a stance; think only of cutting. Make the stance large or small according to what advantage requires. Upper, middle and lower are the stances of the body itself; the two side stances are the flexible ones. The right and left side stances are used where the space above or to one side is blocked, and which one to choose depends on the place. The great principle of this Way says that the ultimate of stance is the middle; understand that the middle stance is the true intent of stance. Look at strategy on a grand scale: the middle stance is the position of the general, and the other four are the subordinate formation that follows him. Study this carefully.
sections.gist: There are five stances, all serving to cut; the middle stance is the commander's base from which the other four take their place.
sections.lesson: Choose your approach from several options, but keep the central goal as the anchor. Adapt the method to the situation without losing sight of the purpose.

en: To know the path of the blade means this: even when you swing a sword you carry yourself, if you know its path well, you can swing it freely. When you try to swing a sword quickly, the path goes wrong and it becomes hard to swing. A sword should be swung at the speed at which it swings well. A fan or a short knife is swung fast, and when you apply that same haste to a sword, the path is lost; this is called chopping with a short blade, and it will not cut a person with a real sword. When you lower the blade, lift it along a path that lifts easily; when you swing it sideways, bring it back along a path that returns easily. Stretch your elbows wide and swing with force. This is the path of the blade. When you learn and practice the five forms of my school, the path of the blade becomes settled and the sword swings well. Train diligently.
sections.gist: Swing the sword at a speed that keeps its path true; haste breaks the path, while a calm, full swing lifts and returns with control.
sections.lesson: Do not push a task faster than its natural rhythm. A steady, full effort done well beats frantic speed that breaks the work apart.

en: First form: the middle stance, with the sword point set against the enemy's face. When you meet the enemy and he strikes at you, slide your blade off to the right and ride over it. When he strikes again, knock his blade down with a turn of the point and leave your sword where it is. When he strikes once more, parry his hands from underneath. This is the first form. Written descriptions alone cannot make the five forms clear; you must take up the sword and practice the path of the blade through these five sword lines. Through them you will know your own path with the blade and be able to read any strike the enemy makes. This teaches that the sword stances are nothing beyond these five. Train in it.
sections.gist: The first form: middle stance with the point at the enemy's face, riding his blade aside, turning the point back and parrying his hands from below.
sections.lesson: When a rival pushes back, redirect their force instead of meeting it head-on, and keep your own momentum. Use their own move to open a path for you.

en: Second form: set the sword in the upper stance, and strike in one blow at the moment the enemy attacks. If the enemy avoids your blow, leave your sword where it is, scoop up from below, and strike the place where he has just attacked. The next blow is the same. Within this form lie many kinds of mind and many rhythms. If you train thoroughly in the whole of this form of our school, you will know the five sword paths in detail and find an opening in any situation. Practice it.
sections.gist: The second form: strike from the upper stance as the enemy attacks; if he evades, scoop up from below and strike again, with many minds and rhythms within.
sections.lesson: When a first attempt misses, follow up at once with a second approach that builds on the opening it left. Persistence with varied timing tends to win.

en: Third form: hold the sword in the lower stance, low and hanging as if carried in the hand. When the enemy strikes, parry his blade from below with your hands. At the moment you parry his hands, when he tries to knock your sword down, pass over his rhythm with a rhythm that overtakes him, and after his strike has landed, cut horizontally across both of his arms. In the lower stance, strike and finish him in one blow at the point where he attacks. Whether you carry the lower stance forward quickly or slowly, you meet him either way. Take up the sword and train.
sections.gist: The third form: lower stance; parry the enemy's hands from below, then cut across his arms once his strike has landed, finishing him in one blow.
sections.lesson: Anticipate the other side's moves and act at the moment they commit. Answer their first step with a precise counter rather than chasing them.

en: Fourth form: hold the sword horizontally in the left side stance. When the enemy strikes, parry his hand from below. With the intent of parrying his hand while he tries to knock your blade down, take his sword's path as it comes, and cut diagonally from above your own shoulder. This is the path of the sword. When the enemy strikes, to receive the path of his blade and win is the principle. Think it over carefully.
sections.gist: The fourth form: left-side stance; parry his hand from below, then cut diagonally down from above your shoulder along the line of his blade.
sections.lesson: Absorb pressure coming from one direction, then answer with a decisive move from the side they did not expect. Reading the flow of a situation often beats direct force.

en: Fifth form: hold the sword horizontally in the right side stance. Read the rhythm of the enemy's attack, and from below the horizontal line on my side, turn the blade diagonally and raise it into the upper stance; then cut straight down from above. This too is to know the path of the blade. Once these forms are trained, a heavy sword can be swung freely. The five forms are not described in full detail here. Through the outline of my school you come to know the path of the blade and the general rhythms. First, these five forms teach you to see the enemy's blade and never leave the hands idle. Even in combat, keep this sword path unbroken: receive the enemy's intent and win with varied rhythms in any way. Consider carefully.
sections.gist: The fifth form: right-side stance; lift the blade from below into the upper stance and cut straight down, which makes even a heavy sword free to swing.
sections.lesson: Build your fundamentals until heavy tasks feel light. Practice the basics until a difficult challenge can be handled with ease.

en: Having a stance and having no stance: holding the sword does not mean you must necessarily assume a fixed stance, but if you place the blade in one of the five positions, a stance results. The sword should be set wherever the enemy's opening and the place require; whichever position it takes, the aim is to cut the enemy cleanly. An upper stance, when adjusted to the moment, drops a little and becomes middle; a middle stance raised slightly for advantage becomes upper. The lower stance is the same: lifted a little as the position requires, it becomes middle. If the side stances move a little toward the center to suit the position, they become middle or lower. Therefore a stance exists, yet there is no fixed stance; this is the principle.

First: once you take up the sword, in every case you must intend to cut the enemy. When the enemy's blade comes and you think of receiving it, parrying it, meeting it, binding it, or touching it, every one of these is a means of cutting him. If you think only 'I receive', 'I parry', 'I meet', 'I bind', or 'I touch', your cut will fall short. In all things it is essential to regard each movement as a means of cutting. Study well.
In strategy on a large scale, even the arrangement of troops is a stance, and all of it serves to win battles. To fix yourself in one place is bad. Study this well.
sections.gist: Stances are fluid: each position shifts into another with small adjustments, and every stance, and every contact, is a means of cutting the enemy.
sections.lesson: Make your plans flexible: move between approaches as needed without losing your central aim. Tie every action back to the goal of winning.

en: Striking with a single beat: the single beat means this. When you reach a position where you and the enemy are close enough to strike, and you seize the moment while the enemy has not yet noticed, you do not move your body and you do not show your intention; you strike immediately, quickly and straight. This is the single-beat strike. It is the rhythm of striking before the enemy has any thought of drawing back, evading, or striking himself. Master this single beat first, then train to strike quickly in the spaces between beats.
sections.gist: The single-beat strike: when you are close and the enemy is unaware, strike at once without moving the body or showing intent.
sections.lesson: When the moment is right and the other party is unprepared, act at once with a clear, direct decision. Hesitation hands over the opening.

en: The two-remaining rhythm (ni no koshi): when I am about to strike and the enemy pulls back quickly, springing back like a drawn bow, make it appear that I am striking. Then strike at the point where his tensed body goes slack. Strike as he pulls back and relaxes. This is the two-remaining strike. Written notes alone can hardly teach it; once taught in person, it is understood at once.
sections.gist: The two-remaining strike: feint an attack as the enemy springs back, then strike at the moment his tension slackens.
sections.lesson: Use a small test or signal to make the other side reveal a weakness, then act once they relax. A feint can draw out what a direct push cannot.

terms.en: two-remaining (a feint, then the true strike)

en: The no-thought, no-mind strike: when the enemy is about to strike and I too am about to strike, my body becomes a striking body and my mind becomes a striking mind, and my hands strike, almost without my knowing when, from the void behind, strongly. This is the no-thought, no-mind strike, a great matter in strategy. Such strikes come up again and again in meetings of blades. Learn it well and train in it.
sections.gist: The no-thought, no-mind strike: when both sides are about to strike, body, mind and hands act together without deliberate calculation.
sections.lesson: When both sides are fully committed, rely on trained instincts. Practice until decisive action comes without overthinking.

en: The flowing-water strike: when you and the enemy are locked in a contest of blades, and the enemy tries quickly to withdraw, quickly to slip away, or quickly to knock your blade aside, open both body and mind, and strike from behind your own body with the sword, slowly and with a sense of lingering, like still water, large and strong. If you learn this strike, you will surely strike well. Understanding the enemy's position is essential.
sections.gist: The flowing-water strike: when the enemy tries to break free, open body and mind and strike slowly, large and strong, like still water.
sections.lesson: When a rival is slipping away or pushing back hard, stay calm and expansive and press with steady force. Read their position before you commit.

en: When I strike out and the enemy tries to block my strike or push my blade away, I make my strike a single line: at the head and at the legs both, with one path of the sword, wherever I can reach. This is the strike of connection. Learn this strike thoroughly, and be able to use it at every meeting of blades. Consider the fine details of each contact carefully.
sections.gist: The strike of connection: when the enemy blocks or pushes aside your blade, strike head and legs in one continuous line on the same sword path.
sections.lesson: Link your moves so that one action sets up the next, covering several needs in one decisive sequence. Think through each contact point in advance.

en: The flint-spark strike happens when your sword and the enemy's sword meet at the same moment. You do not lift your own sword at all, but strike with full force. Your legs are strong, your body is strong and your hands are strong; you strike quickly with all three together. Practice this strike again and again, because without practice it is hard to land. Train it thoroughly and it will land with power.
sections.gist: A quick, all-in strike delivered the instant blades meet, driven by legs, body and hands together, and made forceful through repeated training.
sections.lesson: When a decisive moment arrives, commit your whole effort at once instead of hesitating, and build that readiness through repetition before you need it.

en: The red-leaf strike knocks down the enemy's sword so that you can recover your own. Suppose you hold your sword facing the enemy, intending either to strike or to parry. The strike then comes from a mind of no-thought and no-intent (munen musō), or it is a flint-spark strike. Hit the enemy's sword hard and keep your blade on it, pressing so that the point drops. When you do this, the enemy's sword will certainly fall. This strike becomes easy with practice, so train it thoroughly.
sections.gist: Strike the enemy's blade hard and stay pressed on it with the point lowered, so his sword falls; the technique becomes easy with practice.
sections.lesson: When an obstacle is pressing on you, lean firmly on its core and stay with it until it gives way, rather than making many weak attempts that let it recover.

sections.title_en: The sword that takes the body's place
en: This may be called the sword that takes the place of the body. In general, when you strike an enemy, sword and body do not both move at once. Depending on how the enemy attacks, you send the body in first and the sword follows, paying no attention to the body but going where it needs to. If the body does not move, you can strike with the sword alone, but in most cases you send the body ahead and let the sword come after. Study this carefully and practice the strike.
sections.gist: When striking, send the body forward first and let the sword follow; choose the order according to how the enemy attacks.
sections.lesson: In a demanding task, move your presence and commitment first and let the tools and details follow, adjusting the order to what the situation requires.

en: There are two things here, striking and hitting. To strike means that, whatever the blow, you commit to it with certainty, having fixed your intention on it. Hitting means arriving at the target with force, to the degree that the enemy may die at once; that too is called hitting. To strike is to strike with awareness, knowing what you are doing. Consider this carefully.

When the enemy's hand or foot is hit, there is first contact. After contact, you strike hard so as to follow through. Contact is a feeling like brushing against something. Once both are mastered they are quite separate matters. Work this out for yourself.
sections.gist: Striking is a committed, deliberate blow, while hitting is arrival with force; contact with a limb is first a light touch, followed by a hard follow-through.
sections.lesson: Separate the act of making contact from the decisive follow-through, so you know whether you have truly reached the goal or only brushed against it.

en: The short-armed monkey body means a mind that does not extend the hands. When you enter against the enemy, you do not put out your hands at all; as the enemy strikes, you quickly bring your whole forward body in. When you think of reaching out with a hand, the body always pulls away, so you move the entire body in quickly. At the distance where you can parry hand to hand, the body enters with ease. Study this carefully.
sections.gist: Enter against the enemy by moving the whole body in quickly rather than reaching out with the hands, since extending the arms makes the body draw back.
sections.lesson: When you want to reach someone or something, commit your whole self rather than sending only a hand, since a partial reach tends to pull you back.

en: The sticky-lacquer body means to adhere when you enter close, and not to separate. As you press in on the enemy, attach your head, your body and your legs firmly to the point where you bind. Most people push their face and feet in quickly, but their body pulls back. Fasten your body fully onto the enemy's, leaving not the slightest gap between the two bodies. Study this carefully.
sections.gist: Once inside an opponent's guard, attach the head, body and legs to him with no gap, so the body does not lag behind the limbs.
sections.lesson: Once you engage, close the distance fully so your whole effort moves together, rather than having your hands and attention advance while your body holds back.

en: In any entry against an enemy, do not let your body shrink. Lengthen your legs, extend your hips, reach your neck upward, and press in strongly. Set your face level with the enemy's face and compare your height against his. When you rise high enough to feel you have won, press in hard. This is the crucial point. Consider it well.
sections.gist: On closing with an enemy, keep the body fully extended, rise to face level, and press in forcefully once you feel you hold the higher position.
sections.lesson: In a face-off, do not shrink from the confrontation; stand tall, hold your ground, and press forward once you feel you have the upper position.

en: When the enemy strikes and you also strike, and he receives your sword, your blade sticks to his as you enter. Stickiness means the blades are hard to part, and it should not be forceful. Stick to the enemy's sword as you enter; you may enter as calmly as you like without harm. Stickiness and entanglement are two different things: stickiness is firm, entanglement is weak. Keep this distinction in mind.
sections.gist: Keep your blade adhering to the opponent's as you enter, firm but not forceful; this firm stickiness differs from weak entanglement.
sections.lesson: Hold a point of contact firmly and calmly so you are not easily shaken off, but do not clutch so tightly that you become tangled and weak.

en: The body strike means entering close to the enemy and hitting him with your body. Turn your face slightly aside, thrust your left shoulder out, and strike the enemy's chest. Strengthen your body as much as you can, and make the strike in the rhythm of the breath, with a springing spirit, so that you bounce off together. Once you have mastered this entry, the enemy will spring back several ken (a ken is about 1.8 meters). The strike is strong enough to nearly kill him. Train thoroughly.
sections.gist: Enter close and strike with the body and left shoulder, timed to the breath; a well-trained entry throws the opponent back several meters.
sections.lesson: Some confrontations are won by timing a committed push to the moment of contact, not by pushing harder for longer.

en: The three parries: when you have entered against the enemy and he strikes out with his sword, meet it with your sword in a way that threatens his eyes, and draw the enemy's blade sideways over your right shoulder. Second is the thrust-parry: as the enemy's sword comes, thrust toward his right eye, with the intent of clamping his neck, and receive the blow there. Third, when the enemy strikes with a short blade, enter and receive it without worrying much about your own sword; use your left hand to strike the enemy's face. Form the left hand into a fist and punch at his face. Train thoroughly in these.
sections.gist: Three ways to defend while entering: draw the blade across the shoulder, a thrust-parry aimed at the eye and neck, or punch the face with a clenched left fist.
sections.lesson: When pressed, have several defences ready and fall back on the one that fits the moment, including the simplest direct action.

en: Stabbing at the face means that, when the blades are crossed and the space between the enemy's sword and yours is close, you thrust your sword point at his face. Keep this always in mind, as it is essential. If you hold the intention of piercing his face, his face and body will be drawn forward. If you draw the enemy into leaning forward, there are many ways to gain the advantage. Study this carefully.
In battle, if the enemy's body is drawn forward by over-commitment, that is a quick path to victory. Therefore do not forget the face-stab. Practice this advantage in your regular training.
sections.gist: When blades cross, thrust the point at the opponent's face; the threat draws his body forward and opens him to a quick win.
sections.lesson: Make a direct, visible threat to draw out a reaction; when someone leans into it, that over-commitment exposes the openings you need.

en: Stabbing at the heart means that, in battle, when there are obstructions above or on the sides so that cutting is impossible, you thrust at the enemy. Show him the spine of your blade directly, pull the sword back so the point does not wobble, and thrust at his chest. This is also the mind of deflecting the enemy's cut. It is especially useful when you are tired, or when your sword will not cut well. Consider it carefully.
sections.gist: When overhead or side obstacles block cutting, thrust straight at the chest with the blade spine shown; this also works when tired or when the blade is dull.
sections.lesson: When the usual approach is blocked, switch to a simpler, straighter action that still gets the result, instead of forcing the blocked route.

en: Katsu-totsu: whenever you launch a strike to bring the enemy down, and it looks as if he will strike back, thrust upward from below as if piercing him, and return with a strike. Both are done in a quick rhythm. The raised point carries the intent of thrusting, so intending to thrust and lifting make two beats of one strike. This rhythm always comes up in an exchange of blows. Practice it well and examine it.
sections.gist: In a quick katsu-totsu exchange, when the enemy is about to counter, thrust up from below and strike back in a two-beat rhythm that appears in every exchange.
sections.lesson: When someone pushes back, answer with a quick two-part move, a short thrust then a follow-up, rather than waiting to absorb the full force of the reply.

en: The smacking parry is used when the two swords clash and make a tan-tan beat. Meet the enemy's cut on your sword and strike his blade. The mind of meeting is not to grip tightly, nor merely to receive. Answer the enemy's cut by smacking his sword, and strike him faster than the smack itself. Taking the lead through the smack and then through the strike is essential. If you master the smacking rhythm, however hard the enemy strikes, your blade tip will not drop even a little. Study and practice this.
sections.gist: Meet the enemy's cut with a quick smacking contact on his blade, followed by a faster strike, so your blade stays firm even against heavy blows.
sections.lesson: When hit hard, meet the force with a crisp, well-timed response rather than resisting stiffly or yielding, and keep your own momentum.

en: Position against many is for fighting many people at once. Draw your long and short swords, open them wide to the left and right, and hold them level. Even if enemies come from every direction, drive them toward one side. When they come, look at their order, front and rear, and quickly meet first the one who advances first. Keep your eyes wide and take the moment of the enemy's strike to cut with both swords together: the sword that goes forward cuts the enemy in front, and the sword that returns cuts the enemy coming at your side. Waiting with the swords idle is bad. Quickly settle into the two flank positions, and when enemies come in, cut hard and break them in the direction they come from, then turn back at once toward the direction they came. Always set the enemies up so they press in like fish strung on one line; when you see them piling up, strike hard into them with no gap for them to slip through.

Also, if you think of the enemy only as coming from where he seems to come, and wait expecting that, you cannot move. Read the enemy's rhythm, know the point where his formation collapses, and win. When you often draw many enemies close and drive them into one another, and grasp this mind, then one or ten or twenty enemies are no trouble. Practice well and study.
sections.gist: Against several opponents, hold both swords wide and level, meet the first attacker, cut with both blades in turn, and keep the enemies bunched together.
sections.lesson: When many demands arrive at once, stay composed with a wide view, deal with the first thing that reaches you, and keep the crowd in front of you rather than letting it surround you.

en: The advantage in an exchange of blows is the place where one learns to recognize the winning point in swordsmanship. It is not written out in detail here; through diligent practice you will come to know the points of victory. In general, this is the sword that reveals the true path of the sword art.
Oral transmission (kuden).
sections.gist: Mastering the exchange of blows lets you recognize the decisive points of victory; it cannot be fully written down and must be learned through practice.
sections.lesson: Some skills can only be learned by doing; read the principles, but test them against real situations until you can recognize the winning moment yourself.

en: Through this idea of one strike you surely attain victory. Without studying the sword art well, it is hard to grasp. If you train this principle diligently, strategy becomes a matter of the mind itself, and you win in the way you wish. Practice thoroughly.
sections.gist: Through the single-strike principle, a diligent practitioner gains reliable victories and can win as the mind directs.
sections.lesson: Focus on one decisive action at a time and execute it well; a single clear move, practiced until automatic, often beats a scattered effort.

en: The mind of direct transmission is what is received and passed on from the true path of the Two-Sword One School. Train it thoroughly; making this method part of your own body is essential.
Oral transmission (kuden).
sections.gist: The direct-transmission stance is the inherited core of the school's true path; mastery requires training until the method becomes part of the body.
sections.lesson: Valuable methods are learned from a teacher and made your own through repetition; receive the core of what works and practice it until it feels natural.

en: What is written in this scroll is, in broad outline, the sword art of the single school. Those who take up a sword and learn to win over people must first know the five forms, and through them the five stances, and learn the path of the sword. Then the whole body becomes free, the mind becomes alert, the rhythm of the Way appears, and the hands, sword, body and legs move in accord with the mind. At that stage you can win over one person, then two, and begin to know what is good and bad in strategy. Practice each article of this book one by one, and in fighting the enemy gain the advantage step by step. Take your time, keep the method in mind, and understand that this is the duty of the warrior. Today defeat yesterday's self; tomorrow defeat lesser opponents; afterward defeat the more skilled, following this book without letting your heart wander onto side paths. However many enemies you defeat, if it goes against what was taught, it is not the true path. When this advantage arises in your mind, one body can prevail over dozens, and with the wisdom of the sword you will grasp some portion of the art. A thousand days of practice is the forging; ten thousand days is the refining. Study this carefully. Written on the 13th day of the fifth month of Shōhō 2 (1645) by Shinmen Musashi for Terao Magonojō; dated the 5th day of the second month of Kanbun 7 (1667) by Terao Musei Katsunobu (seal) for Yamamoto Gensuke.
sections.gist: Closing advice: learn the five forms and stances, free the body, work through each article in turn, and beat yesterday's self, not just the enemy.
sections.lesson: Improve steadily by mastering one principle at a time and measuring yourself against your past performance, not only against others, so discipline lasts for years.

sections.title_en: Preface to the Fire Scroll (hi no maki)
en: This is the Two-Sword, One-Stream strategy. I take the matter of fighting and treat it as fire, and I set down the matter of contests in this scroll, which I call the Fire Scroll. Most people think of the advantages of strategy as small. Some know the gain of a wrist motion of five or three sun with the fingertips. Some take up a folding fan and learn the first and second moves from the elbow. Others pick up a sliver of quickness from stance and footwork, training the hands and feet and concentrating on whichever small gain comes first. In my strategy, I stake my life on many contests fought in earnest, and I separate the two principles of life and death. I learn the way of the sword, measure the strength of an enemy's cut, understand the use of the blade's edge and back, and temper myself to kill. To think that small and weak things count for little, or to recall minor advantages while fully armored, is not the point at all. In a fight where each exchange may cost my life, one against five or ten, the surest path to victory is the Way of my strategy. Is there really any difference between one man beating ten and a thousand beating ten thousand? Examine this carefully.

Yet in ordinary daily practice one cannot gather a thousand or ten thousand people to learn this Way. Even taking up a single sword alone, one can weigh the enemy's stratagems, judge his strength and his methods, and use the wisdom and virtue of strategy to reach the point of defeating a crowd. Become skilled in this Way, and hold firmly to the conviction that my direct Way is one whose equal no one in the world could claim, and which no one could finally master more completely. Forge it in the morning and temper it in the evening, refine it until it is complete, and afterwards you gain freedom of self alone. Within you appear extraordinary power and a kind of wondrous strength. This is the living breath by which soldiering is carried on.
sections.gist: Musashi says strategy must be tested in real, life-and-death contests rather than shown off in small skills, and it is mastered through serious daily training.
sections.lesson: Don't judge a skill by how impressive it looks in practice. Test it against real stakes and drill it daily until it holds up under pressure.

terms.en: strategy; the Way of the warrior

en: Reading the place means assessing your position on the ground. In any place there is the matter of keeping the sun at your back, so stand with the sun behind you. If the lay of the land does not allow that, put the sun on your right side. The same holds indoors, where you set the light behind you or on the right. So that your rear is not cramped, open the space on the left and draw in the space on the right as you set your stance. At night, when the enemy is visible, put the fire behind you and the light on your right, and understand this in the same way. Set yourself as if looking down on the enemy, even from a slightly higher spot. Indoors, count the seat of honor as the high place. When the fighting begins and you drive the enemy around, direct him toward your left. Make him stand with his back to rough ground, and drive him toward difficult ground wherever you can.

Do not let the enemy see the ground. Keep him occupied, do not let him turn his face to look about, and press him without any slack. Indoors it is the same: drive him toward the threshold, the lintel, the sliding door, the edge of the veranda, or a pillar, and never let him see where he stands. In every case the aim is to push the enemy onto poor footing or toward obstacles at his flank, and to use the advantage of the ground to win the place. Study this carefully and train at it in earnest.
sections.gist: Choose your position so that light, terrain and space favor you, and push the opponent toward poor footing and obstacles where he cannot see what is happening.
sections.lesson: Before a negotiation or meeting, choose the setting and seating that favor you, and steer the other side toward the points where they are weakest.

sections.title_en: The Three Initiatives (san tsu no sen)
en: The three initiatives. The first is the initiative of attack (kake no sen), where I strike at the enemy first. The second is the initiative of waiting (matsu no sen), where the enemy attacks me and I seize the moment. The third is the initiative of meeting (tai tai no sen), where the enemy and I attack each other at the same time. These are the three initiatives, and at the start of any fight there is nothing beyond them. Since a victory is decided by who takes the initiative first, initiative is the foremost principle of strategy. It has many fine details, but what counts is choosing the right principle for the moment and reading the enemy's mind with the wisdom of my strategy. These cannot be written out in every particular.

First, the initiative of attack. When I am about to attack, I stay calm and then go in suddenly and quickly. Or I make the upper body strong and quick while keeping something in reserve at the base. Or I make the heart truly firm, keep the feet at their normal pace but slightly faster, slip quickly alongside the enemy and throw him into disorder. Or I let go of thought and press the enemy with the same force from beginning to end, so that the strength reaches to the very bottom. All of these are the initiative of attack.

Second, the initiative of waiting. When the enemy comes at me, I pay it no mind and let myself look weak. As he gets close, I suddenly break away with force, as if leaping aside. Then, the moment I see his looseness, I attack at once and win. That is one way. Or, when the enemy attacks, I also grow stronger, and at the instant his rhythm of attack shifts, I receive it and win on the spot. This is the principle of the initiative of waiting.

Third, the initiative of meeting. When the enemy attacks quickly, I answer with calm, strong force and aim at his weak point as he comes near, then defeat him firmly. If he attacks calmly, I watch how he moves. With my body light and moving a little quicker, I go in. When he comes close, I press once, then follow the change in his expression and press strongly. This is the initiative of meeting.

These matters resist clear explanation. Use this writing as a rough guide and work out the larger picture. Although one may always attack first from one's own side, depending on the moment and the principle, it is better, when possible, to attack first and turn the enemy around. In each of these three, initiative rests on the strength of strategic judgment, and you will win by it. Drill it thoroughly.
sections.gist: There are three ways to take the initiative: attack first, answer an attack, or meet the attack together. Each is chosen by reading the moment.
sections.lesson: Decide whether to move first, wait and respond, or meet the other side halfway based on the situation, and aim to be the one who sets the pace.

en: Pinning the pillow means not letting the enemy raise his head. In contests of strategy, being steered about and trailing your opponent is a poor position; I want to move the enemy freely in every way. The enemy thinks the same, and I too have that intent, but neither side will accept the other's moves. So in strategy you block the openings the enemy would strike, press down the thrust he would make, and break away his grip when he tries to hold you. Pinning the pillow means this: once I have attained the true Way and meet the enemy in an exchange, I perceive his intention before he can carry it out. Before his action takes shape, I seize the head of his strike, so he cannot follow through. Take the 'u' of uchi (strike) and hold its beginning. Likewise seize the 'ka' of kakaru (to attack), the 'to' of tobu (to leap), and the 'ki' of kiru (to cut). All of these share one mind. Let the enemy's useless motions go, and suppress the ones that would serve him, so that he cannot make them. That is the specialty of strategy. This is also the mind that tries to suppress what the enemy does, and it works from behind. Better is to move first. While I act according to the Way, at the moment the enemy thinks of acting I catch the head of his intention, so that nothing he does is of use, and I subdue him. That is the skill of a master of strategy, earned through long training. Examine pinning the pillow with great care.
sections.gist: Stop the opponent's plan before it becomes action, by reading the first sign of his move and blocking its beginning.
sections.lesson: Spot a rival's or colleague's plan at its earliest stage and address it before it develops, rather than reacting after it is already moving.

terms.en: pinning the pillow: stopping the enemy's action before it forms

en: Taking a ford, for instance, means crossing the sea at a narrow strait, or crossing a long stretch of water forty or fifty ri wide at its crossing point. In a person's life, too, there are many crossings to make in a single lifetime. On a voyage, you learn where the crossing lies, know the state of your vessel and the swells of the day, and then take what the moment gives you, even without a companion ship. Sometimes you rely on a beam wind, sometimes on a following wind. Even if the wind turns against you, you row two or three ri to reach harbor, knowing that you will arrive. Grasping this, you should cross life's sea with the mind of treating every great turning point as a crossing.

In fighting, too, crossing the ford is essential. Read the enemy's position, recognize your own strengths, and by that understanding cross at the right point, as a skilled navigator crosses a sea route. Once you have made the crossing, you can settle in at ease. To cross the ford is to strike at the enemy's weak point and set yourself on favorable ground. Large victories are won this way. The mind of crossing the ford is needed in both grand strategy and small. Examine it thoroughly.
sections.gist: Like a sailor waiting for the right wind and tide, act at the decisive moment when conditions favor you, and keep adjusting if they change.
sections.lesson: Don't launch a big move until you have read the conditions, the timing and your own strength. Once committed, keep adjusting as the winds shift.

en: Reading the momentum is the province of grand strategy. Know the rise and fall of the enemy, understand the mind of his troops, take in the lay of the ground, and read the enemy's momentum. Then decide how to deploy your own forces. By the principle of strategy, see clearly where victory lies, grasp the initiative with that understanding, and only then engage. In one-on-one fighting too, you must understand the opponent's currents and his character, find his strengths and weaknesses, and set up a move that differs from what his face expresses. Know well the give and take of his rhythm, and take the initiative in the interval it leaves. This is essential. The momentum of things, when your wisdom is strong, will necessarily show itself. Once you are free in the Way of strategy, calculating the enemy's mind well opens many paths to victory. Consider this carefully.
sections.gist: Read the opponent's rise and fall and the flow of the contest, and move when the rhythm favors you rather than when you feel impatient.
sections.lesson: Watch a market's or team's momentum and timing before committing resources. The signs of a shift are usually visible to a careful observer.

terms.en: momentum; the signs of a contest rising or falling

sections.title_en: Pressing Down the Sword (ken o fumu)
en: Pressing down the sword is a principle used exclusively in strategy. First, in grand strategy: when the enemy looses arrows and fires guns at us, and then attacks in the wake of his volleys, it becomes hard for us to get in close if we are busy reloading guns and nocking arrows. The mind is to close quickly while the enemy is still shooting. Once you are near, he cannot nock another arrow or fire another gun. Whatever the enemy does, if you seize the advantage at that very moment and press down on what he is doing, you win.

In one-on-one fighting too: if I strike only after the enemy's blade has landed, my blow arrives a beat late and gets nowhere. The sword he drives out should be pressed down the instant it leaves him, so that he cannot make a second stroke. This pressing is not limited to the feet. Press with the body, press with the mind, and of course press with the sword, so that the enemy cannot strike again. This is the principle of initiative in all things. It does not mean meeting him head-on in a single collision. It means following directly behind him. Examine this thoroughly.
sections.gist: Strike the instant the opponent begins his attack, so that he has no room to follow up with a second blow.
sections.lesson: When a rival makes a move, respond at once so they cannot easily repeat it. Don't give the other side a second chance to regroup.

terms.en: pressing down the sword at its start

en: Collapse is present in all things. A house collapses, a body collapses, and the enemy collapses too, when the rhythm goes awry at the moment of contact and things come apart. In grand strategy, you must catch the enemy's disordered rhythm and pursue him without letting the gap slip by. If you do not follow through when his line breaks, he will rebuild and turn back on you. In one-on-one fighting as well, when the enemy's timing falters and a sign of breaking appears, you must not look away. If you slacken even for a moment, he recovers and becomes fresh again. It is essential to pursue him at the very mark of his collapse, so that he cannot restore his footing or his posture.

Pursuit calls for a plainly strong mind. Strike him away so that he has no chance to rise and come back, and understand well what it means to strike away. If you stay stuck to him, your mind goes slack. Work on this.
sections.gist: When the opponent's rhythm breaks and he starts to collapse, press on without pause so he cannot regain his footing.
sections.lesson: When a competitor stumbles, push the advantage quickly and steadily rather than easing off, or they will regroup and come back stronger.

en: Becoming the enemy means thinking with your own body as if you stood in his place. Look at the world: a thief who holes up in a house is seen by people as a formidable foe. Thinking as the enemy, you feel that everyone in the world is against you and that there is no way out. The one who shuts himself inside is the pheasant; the one who goes in to finish him is the hawk. Examine this well. Even in grand strategy, when you regard the foe as a foe, you think of him as strong and handle the matter with great care.

If you have good troops, understand the principles of strategy well, and know how to win over the enemy, there is no need to worry about the path to victory. In one-on-one fighting too, put yourself in the enemy's place. Against a man who understands strategy well, reasons firmly and is skilled in the Way, you must assume you will lose, and think accordingly. Hold this in mind and consider it deeply.
sections.gist: Put yourself in the opponent's position and assume he is strong and determined, so you never underestimate him.
sections.lesson: Imagine how a rival or a difficult client sees the situation before you plan. Assuming they are capable keeps you from careless mistakes.

terms.en: becoming the enemy in one's mind

sections.title_en: Breaking the Locked Hands (yotsude o hanasu)
en: Releasing the four hands means that when you and the enemy press against each other with the same spirit, and neither side can gain ground, the strategy goes nowhere. If you find yourself locked in such mutual pressure, drop the mind at once and win by another advantage. In grand strategy too, when the situation becomes a deadlocked tangle of forces, nothing advances, and this is what others criticize. Quickly let go of that mind and win through an advantage the enemy does not foresee. In one-on-one fighting too: if you feel yourself sliding into a locked contest, change your mind right then, take up the enemy's position, and through a completely different advantage recognize how to win. Think it through carefully.
sections.gist: When both sides are locked in the same stubborn struggle and neither can advance, drop that approach and win another way.
sections.lesson: If a negotiation or argument has stalled into deadlock, abandon the same tactic and find a different angle the other side does not expect.

terms.en: the four hands; a locked deadlock

en: Stirring the shadow is used when the enemy's intention cannot be made out. In grand strategy, if you cannot read the enemy's position at all, show him strong pressure from your side and watch how he responds. Once you have seen his response, win by a different advantage, which is easy then.
