In one-on-one fighting as well, when the enemy holds his sword behind or off to the side and his intention is hidden from you, make a sudden feint. The enemy's intent will come out in his blade. Once it is revealed, seize the advantage right then and know victory for certain. If you are careless, the rhythm slips away. Examine this well.
sections.gist: When you cannot read the opponent's intention, apply a probing pressure and watch how he responds. His reaction will reveal his plan.
sections.lesson: If you cannot tell what a counterpart wants, make a probing move and watch how they react. Their reaction will show you their plan.

terms.en: the hidden intent; stirring the shadow

sections.title_en: Holding Down the Shadow (kage o osaeru)
en: Holding down the shadow is used when the enemy's intention to press from his side is visible. In grand strategy, when he tries to carry out his action, press down his advantage. If you show him strongly that you will suppress it, the force of your display pushes him and his mind changes. Change your own mind too, and from a mind without fixed thoughts, initiate first and win. In one-on-one fighting: stop the enemy's rising, strong intent with the rhythm of your own advantage. At the moment his rhythm stops, seize the advantage and initiate first. Think about this carefully.
sections.gist: When the opponent's intention is visible, press against his move so he changes course, then take the initiative yourself.
sections.lesson: When you can see a rival about to act, put a check on their plan to shift their approach, then move on the opening that results.

en: Passing on the mood is found in all things. Drowsiness passes from one person to another, yawning passes, and time itself can pass on. In grand strategy, when the enemy is agitated and hurries, eager to press, do not mind it at all. Show complete calm and an unhurried air, and the enemy takes this on and relaxes as well. When you see his slackness, attack from a mind without fixed thoughts, quickly and strongly, and win. In one-on-one fighting too: relax your body and mind, wait for the enemy's moment of looseness, and attack first, strongly and quickly. The advantage of initiative is the essence here.
There is also a related matter, the making of weakness, which resembles this. One is the mind of boredom, one is the mind of carelessness, and one is the mind of softening. Study these well.
sections.gist: Moods and rhythms pass from one person to another. By staying calm yourself, you can make the opponent relax, then strike in the gap.
sections.lesson: Stay composed when others are rushed or anxious. Their tension eases, a gap opens, and that is when a decisive action will work.

terms.en: to pass on a mood or rhythm

en: Provoking is present in all things. The first is a mind poised on the knife's edge; the second is a forced, unreasonable mind; the third is a mind of the unexpected. Consider each carefully.

In grand strategy, provoking is essential. Strike suddenly with force at the place the enemy does not expect, before his mind has settled, and take the initiative with your advantage to win. In one-on-one fighting: begin by showing a relaxed, gentle manner, then press suddenly and hard. While the enemy's mind is catching up and shifting, do not let the opening slip. Seize the advantage and win on the spot. Think it over carefully.
sections.gist: Unsettle the opponent with unexpected, edgy or unreasonable-looking moves, then strike while he is off balance.
sections.lesson: Surprise a competitor with a bold but reasoned move they did not anticipate, and act before they can settle their thinking again.

en: Being startled happens in all things: a mind is frightened by something unforeseen. In grand strategy, to startle the enemy is not just a matter of what lies right before his eyes. It may come from a sound, or from making something small look large, or from a sudden attack from the flank. These startle him. Take advantage of the moment of fright and win through it. In one-on-one fighting too: startle with your body, startle with the sword, startle with your voice, and attack in a way the enemy never imagined. Take the benefit of his startled state and win on the spot. Examine this well.
sections.gist: Frighten the opponent with a sudden noise, apparent size, or an attack from an unexpected side, then win while he is startled.
sections.lesson: A sudden, well-timed change in approach can unsettle a rival, but use surprise to make a clear step forward, not just to rattle people.

en: Mabururu means that when you and the enemy are close, you press hard against each other, and if neither side can break through, you stay tangled with him just as you are. Inside that tangle, the key is to win by seizing the advantage. In large-scale strategy as well, when both armies push at each other and neither gains a decisive edge, mix in with the enemy so that neither side can separate. Within that, gain the benefit, recognize the advantage, and press forward firmly; this is essential. Examine it carefully.
sections.gist: When both sides are too close to separate, do not break off. Stay locked in, and win from inside the struggle by seizing whatever advantage appears.
sections.lesson: In a deadlocked negotiation or a tight rivalry, stay engaged in the details instead of pulling away, and watch for the small edge that tips the outcome.

terms.en: entangling; closing in and mixing with the enemy

en: Touching a corner means that when you push against something strong, you cannot simply force it straight in. In large-scale strategy, read the enemy's formation, press at a strong corner of his line, and you will gain its benefit. As a corner gives way, the whole body tends to give way with it, so among the many corners you must understand each one and seize the victory it offers; this is essential. In small-scale fighting too, if you cause pain at a corner of the enemy's body and his stance grows weaker and begins to crumble, victory comes easily. Examine this carefully and be sure you recognize the place to win.
sections.gist: Strong things cannot be forced straight on. Find the weak corner of the opponent's position, press there, and the rest of his stance will start to collapse.
sections.lesson: When a large obstacle or entrenched habit resists head-on pushing, approach its edges or its weakest part instead, where progress is easier and the rest gives way.

terms.en: corner; edge of the enemy's formation or stance

en: Uromekasu means keeping the enemy from having a settled mind. In large-scale strategy on the battlefield, read the enemy's state of mind and, using your strategic judgment, make him uncertain: make him wonder whether your attack comes from here or there, whether you are slow or quick. When his mind begins to waver, catch that beat and secure the place of victory. Also, in one-on-one fighting, at the right moment, use many tactics: make a cut appear as a feint, or a thrust appear as a cut, or make him think you intend to close in. When you catch the moment his mind wavers, you can freely take the place of victory. This is the essence of fighting. Examine it carefully.
sections.gist: Keep the opponent unsure of your next move. When his mind wavers in doubt, he loses the balance needed to defend, and you gain the upper hand.
sections.lesson: In a negotiation or competition, keep rivals guessing about your next move instead of revealing your full plan, and strike when their confidence starts to slip.

en: The three voices are the voice at the beginning, the voice in the middle and the voice at the end, divided into three. Choose the voice to suit the place; this is essential. A voice carries energy, so we raise it against fire, against wind and waves; the voice shows strength. In large-scale strategy, the voice at the start of battle is raised with all the force you can muster. The voice during the fight is pitched low and rises from deep within, and when you prevail, you shout afterward with great strength. These are the three voices.

In one-on-one fighting too, to draw out the enemy, feign a strike and cry 'Ei!' from above your head; the blade comes down only after the cry has left you. And when you have struck the enemy, cry out afterward: this shout announces that you have won. This is called the voice before and after. Never shout at the same instant the sword swings. If you shout during the fight, shout in rhythm, riding the beat. Examine this carefully.
sections.gist: Shout at three moments: before the clash to unsettle the enemy, low during the fight to keep rhythm, and after the cut to announce victory.
sections.lesson: Mark the start, middle and end of a project with a clear signal: state your intent early, keep a steady pace, and celebrate only once the result is earned.

terms.en: voice before and after the cut

en: Magiruru in large-scale battle means that both sides line up their troops against one another. When the enemy is strong, you move in with magiruru: attack one flank, and when you see him start to crumble, leave that flank and attack the next stronger point. The whole movement is like a zigzag path up a mountain. When you bring a large force against many enemies, this same mind is essential: do not attack in only one direction. If they scatter, go after the strong side again, moving in a zigzag, reading the enemy's rhythm and his appearance, and pressing where the position is right. Once you have broken through in that position, press on without hesitation; that is advantageous. When you move in close as well, keep this mind when the enemy is strong. Magiruru means never to step back, not even for a single pace, but to keep moving into the tangle. Consider this well.
sections.gist: Against a strong enemy, do not push into one spot. Hit a weak flank, then shift to the next point, zigzagging through his line, and never retreat a step.
sections.lesson: When one approach stalls, move laterally to another opening rather than pushing harder in the same place; keep advancing and do not back off.

en: Hishigu means that you view the enemy as weak and, standing in your strength, crush him. This is the core idea. In large-scale strategy, when you judge the enemy's rank of troops, or see that although he is numerous his mind is disordered and weakening at that point, crush him: pour your force down from the head onto him, pressing down. If your crushing is weak, he may turn and push back, so think of crushing as if you grip something in your fist. Examine this carefully.

In one-on-one fighting too: when your own skill or position is lacking, or when the enemy's timing is off and he has stepped back, do not lose your breath even a little. Keep your eyes steady and press straight in. The first priority is never to let him rise even a little. Examine this carefully.
sections.gist: When the enemy seems weak or his timing is off, press him hard and without pause, so he cannot recover or rise again.
sections.lesson: When a rival stumbles or a project loses momentum, press the advantage decisively and keep the pressure on, so they cannot regain their footing.

en: The mountain-and-sea mind warns against repeating the same move several times in a fight. Doing something twice cannot always be avoided, but a third try is not advisable. If you have tried a technique and it has not worked, do not use it again; switch at once to a completely different one. If that also fails, then try another entirely different method. So when the enemy expects mountains, strike as the sea; when he expects the sea, strike as mountains. This is the principle of strategy. Examine it carefully.
sections.gist: Do not repeat a technique that has failed twice. Switch to a completely different approach, reversing what the enemy expects: mountain becomes sea.
sections.lesson: If a tactic fails twice, stop repeating it. Change the approach entirely, since the other side has learned to expect your usual move.

en: Piercing the bottom means this: in fighting the enemy, you may seem to win on the surface by using the right technique, yet if the enemy keeps his spirit unbroken, he may be beaten above but not below. In that case, suddenly take on a different mind, drain the enemy's spirit, and attack from below, watching for the moment he collapses. The key is to see that moment. Piercing the bottom can be done with the sword, with the body, or with the mind; it cannot be known in only one way. If he has collapsed from the bottom, you need not hold anything back; otherwise, keep something in reserve. As long as you keep a reserve in mind, the enemy will be hard to break. In both large-scale and small-scale strategy, train thoroughly in piercing the bottom.
sections.gist: A surface win can hide an enemy who has not broken inside. Strike suddenly at his core spirit, and keep a reserve until he truly collapses.
sections.lesson: Looking successful on the surface is not enough; make sure the other side is truly beaten underneath, and keep some reserve until the result is solid.

terms.en: piercing to the bottom; breaking the enemy's inner resolve

en: Renewing means this: when you and the enemy are fighting and your minds become tangled so that no progress can be made, drop your current effort. Shake off your spirit and think of everything as freshly begun, then take the rhythm of that renewed moment and find the victory in it. Whenever you and the enemy are locked in a grip, change your mind completely and win with a different advantage. In large-scale strategy too, knowing how to renew is essential. With the wisdom of strategy this is easy to see. Examine it carefully.
sections.gist: When a contest gets stuck, drop the old approach and start again with a fresh mind; a new rhythm often brings a win that was blocked before.
sections.lesson: When a project or conversation stalls, reset your attitude and approach it as a fresh start rather than pushing harder on the same stuck point.

en: In a fight, when you and the enemy are both preoccupied with small details and your minds become entangled, always hold the rat's head and the ox's neck in mind, repeating the phrase to yourself. Amid the small details, suddenly take on a large mind and shift between large and small. This is one of the essentials of martial strategy, a single mental discipline. A warrior should hold this same image in his everyday mind too. In large-scale or small-scale strategy alike, never let go of this mind. Examine it carefully.
sections.gist: When both sides are lost in tiny details, shift abruptly between a small focus and a big-picture view, and train this switch in daily life too.
sections.lesson: When you are stuck on a small problem, step back to the big picture, then zoom in again. Moving between detail and overview keeps decisions sharp.

terms.en: rat's head, ox's neck: switching between small and large

sections.title_en: Knowing the General and Troops (shōsotsu o shiru)
en: Knowing the general and the troops means this: whenever battle comes, in every step of the path you intend to take, always apply this method. With the wisdom of strategy, regard every enemy as one of your own soldiers, and think of shaping him to your wishes. Think that you can move the enemy freely wherever you like. Here, you are the general and the enemy is the soldier. Work this out for yourself.
sections.gist: In a contest, see yourself as the commander and the opponent as a soldier you can direct. Taking this stance lets you move him where you want.
sections.lesson: Approach a negotiation or competition as the one setting direction rather than only reacting, so the other party's moves become steps you can guide.

en: Releasing the hilt has many meanings. Some minds aim to win even with the hands empty of the blade; others hold the long sword yet need not use it to win. These are many different minds, and they cannot be set down in writing. Train thoroughly.
sections.gist: Letting go of the sword can mean winning without it, or holding a blade without relying on it. These mindsets differ and must be practised, not just read.
sections.lesson: Sometimes the best result comes from not reaching for your usual tool; practise having other options so you are not dependent on one approach.

terms.en: releasing the hilt; letting go of the sword

en: The boulder body means this: once you have gained the path of strategy, you suddenly become like a boulder, a body that nothing strikes and nothing moves, unshaken by any of the myriad affairs.
Oral transmission (kuden).
sections.gist: After mastering strategy, you can become immovable like a boulder: nothing hits you and nothing moves you. The secret of this state is passed on orally.
sections.lesson: Stay calm and steady when pressure hits, so events do not knock you off center. This steadiness is something you practise, not something you have by default.

terms.en: oral transmission; secret teaching passed by word of mouth

en: What I have set down in this scroll is only what has constantly come to my mind within the field of the single school of swordsmanship, and I have spoken of it as it arose. Now, for the first time, I set this benefit down in writing, so the sequence of earlier and later passages is tangled, and it is hard to explain it finely. Still, for the sake of those who will study this path, it may serve as a guide to the heart. From my youth onward I have set my mind on the path of strategy. I have labored at the ordinary techniques of swordsmanship, exhausted my hands and body, and passed through many different states of mind. When I searched out the other schools too, some explained themselves with words and excused their shortcomings, while others performed delicate movements with the hands to look fine in the eyes of onlookers. Not one of them had any true mind. Of course, those who train in this manner think they are disciplining their body and mind, but it becomes a sickness of the path, lingering for generations, and the straight road of strategy grows corrupt in the world; this is the foundation of the path's decline. The sword becomes a true path only when it is used to defeat an enemy in real combat, and this principle must not differ even slightly. If you acquire the understanding in my strategy and walk the straight course, you need have no doubt that you will win. Written on the twelfth day of the fifth month of Shōhō 2 (1645), by Shinmen Musashi, for Terao Magonojō-dono. Dated the fifth day of the second month of Kanbun 7 (1667), Terao Musei Katsunobu (seal), for Yamamoto Gensuke-dono.
sections.gist: Musashi closes: these teachings come from real fighting, not showy technique. Practise the plain, decisive method and trust its result.
sections.lesson: Judge a skill by whether it works in real use, not by how impressive it looks; practise the plain method that delivers results.

sections.title_en: Learning the Ways of Other Schools
en: This scroll, written as notes in the manner of a jotted record, sets out the practices of other lineages. Without knowing the paths of rival traditions, it is hard to see clearly the principles of my own single school. Looking into the martial arts of other lineages, I find some that take up a very long sword and devote themselves to power in its use. Some, which they call the small sword, pursue the Way with a short blade. Others use many different sword techniques and pass on their teaching through fixed postures, calling the outer form the front and the inner teaching the secret. None of these is the true Way. I have set out their faults clearly in the secret section of this scroll, so that good and bad, right and wrong, become known. The reasoning of my own school is different. Other traditions spread themselves across many accomplishments in order to earn a living; they dress things up, make flowers bloom, and fashion goods to sell, so they are not the true Way. Moreover, people in the world reduce strategy to sword-fencing alone, practice only the swinging of the blade and the training of the body, and judge victory by what the hands can manage. None of these is a sound Way. Each shortfall of the other traditions I write out in this book. Study it thoroughly and understand the advantage of the two swords in one school.
sections.gist: Musashi lists the flaws of rival schools so readers can separate true from false and see why his two-sword school differs.
sections.lesson: Before judging any method, learn the alternatives and where they fail. Then you can explain clearly why your own approach works.

en: Some other traditions favor a very large sword. In my strategy I consider these weak schools. The reason is that they do not know the principle that one wins over a person by any means at all. Valuing the length of the blade, they want to win from a distance where the enemy cannot reach, so they tend to prefer long swords. What the world calls an inch of advantage in the hand is the talk of someone who does not understand strategy. So they rely on length and, lacking real method, try to win from afar. This comes from a weak spirit, which is why I regard them as a weak strategy.

If the enemy is close and you are grappling, a long sword cannot be swung for much effect. With little room near the hilt, the long-sword user is inferior to someone who swings a short wakizashi freely. Those who like long swords may give reasons for it, and such reasons exist for them personally, but viewed from the real Way of the world, they are not reasonable. If you carry no long sword and must fight with a short one, you will certainly lose at times. Or in a place with no room overhead or at the sides, or in a setting where only a short blade is at hand, preferring a long sword is a doubtful habit in strategy and a bad state of mind.

Some people are not strong, and some bodies cannot manage a long blade. There is the old saying that the large can encompass the small, but I do not mean to reject the long sword flatly. What I reject is the lean toward the long sword, a narrow attachment. In large-scale strategy, long swords correspond to large numbers and short ones to small numbers. Can small numbers not fight large numbers? There are many examples of few overcoming many. In my school I dislike this kind of narrow, one-sided mind. Consider it carefully.
sections.gist: Preferring a very long sword to win from afar reflects a weak spirit, and in close fighting that length becomes a handicap.
sections.lesson: Do not lean on one advantage that works only from a distance. Build the skill that works up close, where the real decisions are made.

sections.title_en: The Myth of the Strong Sword
en: There should be no such thing as a 'strong sword' or a 'weak sword'. A sword swung with a strong mind is coarse, and coarseness alone does not win. If in cutting a person you try to cut forcefully, the cut will not land. Trying to cut hard during a test cutting is also bad. When facing an opponent whose blade is hard to beat, one cuts with a weak mind and does not think of cutting hard. But when you are trying to kill a person, there is neither a strong mind nor a weak mind. One thinks only of killing until the enemy dies. If you use a strong sword and the enemy's sword is also strong, you will overshoot and surely end up in a bad state. When you strike hard against the enemy's blade, your own sword bends and shatters. Therefore there is no such thing as a 'strong sword'.

In large-scale strategy also, if you hold a strong army in battle and want to win by strength, the enemy holds strong troops and also wants to fight with strength. Both are the same. In all things, victory requires a principle; without principle, victory cannot be achieved. In my Way I do not think of anything unreasonable at all. By the wisdom of strategy I can find places to win in whatever way is needed. Think about this carefully.
sections.gist: There is no 'strong' or 'weak' sword: forcing strength ruins cuts, and the aim is simply to kill with a settled mind.
sections.lesson: When pushing a deal or argument, do not rely on raw pressure. Keep a clear aim and let sound principle decide the outcome.

en: To aim for victory with only a short sword is not the true Way. Since ancient times the sword has been spoken of as long and short, and I explain both. Strong men in the world can swing a large sword lightly, so they have no special liking for the short one. Also, the long sword is used together with spears and long halberds. Choosing a short sword in order to slip through gaps in the enemy's swing, to leap in and grab, reveals a narrowed mind, and that is bad.

Moreover, watching for openings and aiming to respond only after the enemy has acted is a mind I dislike. If you use a short weapon and try to get in close, it does not work when there are many enemies. A short blade used to cut down a crowd, leap about freely, or whirl around ends up as a purely defensive weapon, and one becomes enveloped and tangled. That is not a sure way. Rather, my body should be strong and upright, pursuing the enemy and forcing him to leap and falter, so that the setup is aimed surely at victory. In large-scale strategy the principle is the same: with superior numbers, pin the enemy in a confined space, as at an archery range, and crush him at once. This is the essence of strategy.

People in the world, through constant practice of handing things back and forth, passing and ducking, grow accustomed to these motions, and their minds are pulled along by the way of doing them, so others turn them around. The Way of strategy is straight and correct. It is therefore essential to chase the enemy with correct principle and bring him under control. Consider this carefully.
sections.gist: Relying on a short sword to slip past openings is a narrow, defensive habit; the right way is to press forward and seize the initiative.
sections.lesson: Avoid defensive habits that wait for an opening. Take the initiative, set the terms, and steer the discussion toward your goal instead of reacting to others.

en: To teach a large number of sword techniques to others is to turn the Way into merchandise, and to make beginners think deeply because the count of techniques looks impressive. Strategy dislikes this. The reason is that when you think there are many ways of killing a person, you become confused. In the world there is no other way to kill a person. Whether one knows the craft or not, whether man, woman, or child, striking and cutting is not a path of many forms. If you change it, saying I will hit this way or strike that way, there is no other method. Because this is a path of cutting first, there is no need for a great number of techniques.

But depending on the place and circumstances, for instance when the upper side or the sides are blocked, one should hold the sword so that it does not get caught, and so there is a set of five, which are called the five directions. Beyond that, to add techniques, to twist the hands and body, to leap and spread out in order to cut people, is not the true Way. Cutting by twisting does not cut; cutting by twisting the body does not cut; cutting by leaping does not cut; cutting by spreading out does not cut. In the end these are useless. In my strategy, both body and mind are straight. The aim is to make the enemy's posture distort and warp, and the essential thing is to win through the twisting of his mind. Consider this carefully.
sections.gist: Teaching many techniques makes cutting seem complicated; in truth, cutting has few forms and needs only directness.
sections.lesson: Too many methods can confuse a team. Reduce a complex task to a few essentials, and apply them consistently.

en: Placing great emphasis on fixed postures of the sword is a mistake. Postures would belong only to a time without an opponent. Rules drawn from old precedent or current fashion have no place in the Way of contest. The task is to make the enemy's position bad. In all things, the idea of a stance is to use a point that does not move. Some fortify a castle or set up a camp, holding firm even when others attack; that is an ordinary matter. But in the Way of strategic contest, in everything the mind must be set on taking the initiative. The stance-mind is the mind that waits for the enemy to act first. Consider this carefully.

In the Way of strategy and contest, move the enemy's stance. Do something outside his expectation, make him waver, provoke him, or frighten him. Take advantage of the rhythm when he is disordered, and win. So I dislike the mind of the stance, a passive mind that only reacts. Therefore my Way has the saying 'having a stance and having no stance': there is a stance, and yet there is no stance.

In large-scale strategy too, one must grasp the enemy's numbers, read the nature of the battlefield, know the position of one's own force, and gain its advantage, then form ranks and begin the fight. This is the core of battle. When the enemy has attacked first and we answer, the outcome changes greatly. In handling the sword, hold a sound posture and receive the enemy's blade well. When you feel you can parry well, it is like holding a bristling barrier of spears and halberds. When you strike the enemy, your spirit must be like pulling a stake from a fence and using it as a spear. Examine this closely and cultivate it with careful thought.
sections.gist: Fixed stances suit times when no one is pushing; in real contest, move the enemy's posture and take the initiative.
sections.lesson: Rigid plans are fine when nobody pushes back. In competition, keep options open and respond to what others actually do.

en: Some schools direct the gaze to the enemy's blade, others to his hands, others on his face, others on his feet, and so on. If you fix your gaze deliberately on any one of these, the mind becomes confused, and that is a sickness of strategy. Consider a man playing kemari: he does not stare at the ball, yet by a run of kicks, sliding and rolling the ball, his foot moves by habit without close watching. Likewise, a performer who has mastered his craft can balance a door on his nose or juggle several swords. None of this is deliberate eye-fixing, yet through constant contact with the object he perceives it naturally. In the Way of strategy also, after many encounters, one learns to read each opponent's mind and its lightness and weight, and once the Way is mastered even the distance, speed, and timing of the sword become visible.

The eye that is set on the opponent in my school is the eye that sees into his intent. In large-scale strategy it is the same: watch the enemy's strength as a whole. There are two modes of seeing: the perceiving gaze and the sighting gaze. The perceiving gaze holds strongly on the enemy's spirit, observes the state of the battle, follows the progress of the fight and the shifts of advantage, and sees weakness and strength at each moment. This surely wins. In single combat, do not fix the eyes on small things. As I said, if you fix on details and neglect what matters, your mind becomes confused and victory slips away. Examine this and train it well.
sections.gist: Fixing the eyes on one spot confuses the mind; a master takes in the whole situation and the enemy's intent, not small details.
sections.lesson: Do not fixate on one metric, person, or detail. Keep the whole picture in view and watch for the moment the situation shifts.

en: Regarding footwork, there are many named methods: floating steps, leaping steps, springing steps, treading steps, crow steps, and various rules for each. I see all of these as lacking. I reject floating steps, because in battle the feet tend to float, so they must be planted firmly. I also do not favor leaping steps, since they foster the habit of leaping and a leaping spirit; no matter how many leaps you make, there is no principle behind them, so leaping is bad. Springing steps are hopping steps, and treading steps are waiting steps, which I dislike especially. Beyond these there are various quick steps, such as crow steps. Yet in swamps, marshes, river valleys, stony ground, or thin paths, one fights enemies who are right there, so leaping and springing cannot always be used, and there are places where settled steps cannot be taken.

In my school, footwork does not change. I simply walk as one walks on an ordinary road. Speed and slowness are matched to the enemy's rhythm, the body keeps its posture neither too much nor too little, and the feet never become disordered. Footwork is essential in large-scale strategy as well. If you rush in quickly without understanding the enemy's mind, the rhythm will be off and it is hard to win. And if your steps are too slow and you do not catch the enemy's wavering, you lose the chance to win and cannot finish the contest quickly. You must find the moment the enemy wavers and crumbles, and never give him even a little room to recover. Train well.
sections.gist: Footwork should be ordinary and firm, adjusted to rhythm; leaping, floating, and trick steps are unreliable.
sections.lesson: Keep your foundation steady and match your pace to the situation. Do not hop between trendy tactics that leave you off balance.

en: The matter of speed in strategy is not the true Way. Speed means being out of step with the rhythm of a thing, so something is judged fast or slow. A master of the Way does not appear to be in a hurry.

Some people can cover forty or fifty ri on foot in a day, but that does not mean they run continuously from morning to night. An untrained person may seem to run all day, but his measure is poor. In the Way of the dance-chant, if a skilled singer performs and a novice tries to join in, the novice lags behind and becomes busy. When a drum is beaten to the Old Pine tune, the rhythm is calm, yet the novice falls behind or rushes ahead. The Takasago piece is a quick one, but hurry is bad: it stumbles, it is called falling over, and it misses the beat. Slowness is also bad. Skilled performers seem unhurried, yet keep no gap in their timing. In anything a trained person does, there is no appearance of busyness.

Through these examples, understand the principle of the Way. Speed is especially harmful in strategy, because, depending on the place, such as a swamp or marsh, the body and legs cannot be moved quickly together. Still less can you cut quickly with a long sword in such ground. If you try to cut hurriedly, as though you were wielding a fan or a small knife, you will not cut even a little. Consider this clearly.

In large-scale strategy as well, a hurried and busy spirit is undesirable. Keep the spirit steady, as one holds a pillow in place, and you will never fall behind by a hair. If the opponent is rushing recklessly, act in the opposite manner and remain calm. Do not be swayed by him. Train diligently to attain this spirit.
sections.gist: Hurry is not speed; true skill keeps a steady rhythm and stays calm rather than rushing to match others.
sections.lesson: Rushing to match others' pace causes mistakes. Work at a steady, deliberate rhythm and you will finish sooner, with less rework.

en: In strategy, which is the outer and which the inner? Depending on the art, some speak of inner secrets and hidden keys, but when actually fighting an enemy, the principle is that you fight on the surface and do not cut with some inner secret. My method of teaching is this. For one who is just beginning the Way, I first have him practice forms that are easy to perform and teach the points that are quickly understood. Deeper principles that his mind cannot yet reach, I teach later, gradually, as I see his understanding open. Yet in general there is no entrance into an inner chamber, because one trains by learning the manner of meeting each situation. In the world, when you go into the mountains looking for the inner recesses and keep going deeper, you come back out at the entrance. Every Way has an inner meeting point, and sometimes it is good to show the entrance. In the principle of battle, what should be hidden and what should be revealed?

Therefore, in passing on my Way, I do not favor sworn oaths, written pledges, or threatened punishments. Observing the ability of those who study with me, I teach the direct path and have them abandon the bad habits of the five or six paths of other arts. They naturally enter the true Way of the warrior's law and come to a state without doubt. This is the teaching of my school. Train well.
sections.gist: No hidden inner teaching exists in real combat; train beginners in what they can grasp first, then deepen step by step.
sections.lesson: Do not hoard secret knowledge to feel important. Teach newcomers the basics first, then introduce deeper principles as they are ready.

en: Above, I have set out the martial traditions of other schools in nine articles in the Wind scroll, with their details written in brief. Each of them, from its openings to its inner secrets, could be shown clearly one by one, but I have deliberately not written the name of any school or its great secrets. The reason is that each school has its own view and its own justifications for its Way, and each person has his own ideas. Even within one school there are small differences, so for the benefit of readers in later generations I have not recorded the lines of each school. I have summed up the general nature of other schools in nine points. If one judges the Ways of the world by the straight reasoning of people, then relying on length, or favoring shortness as a principle, or leaning on strength or weakness, or on roughness or fineness, are all crooked ways. So even if I did not reveal the openings and inner teachings of other schools, everyone should already understand them.

In my single school, the sword has no inner and outer teaching, and posture has no fixed form. One knows its virtue only through the mind. This is the essential point of strategy. Set down on the 12th day of the 5th month in Shōhō year two (1645) by Shinmen Musashi, addressed to Terao Magonojo. Dated the 5th day of the 2nd month in Kanbun year seven (1667), with the monogram of Terao Musei Katsunobu, addressed to Yamamoto Gensuke.
sections.gist: Musashi withholds rival names and secrets, since each school has its own reasoning; the nine faults are plain to see.
sections.lesson: Judge rival approaches by their underlying reasoning, not their labels. Honest evaluation keeps revealing the same few weaknesses.

en: The Way of strategy of the two swords, one school, is set out here in the Scroll of the Void. The meaning of void is that in all things there is nothing, and whatever is not known is regarded as void. Of course the void is absent. Knowing what is present, one knows what is absent; that is the void.

In the world, people look at things poorly and take not-understanding as void. That is not the true void, but a confusion of the mind. In the Way of strategy too, warriors who study think that whatever they cannot grasp in their craft is void. That is not real emptiness at all. A warrior who wishes to reach the strategic Way must study the other martial arts thoroughly and not stray a hair's breadth from the warrior's path. With a settled spirit, build up your training every day and every hour. Polish the heart and mind, the two spirits, and sharpen the two modes of seeing, the perceiving eye and the sighting eye. When the spirit is not clouded in the least, when the cloud of confusion has cleared away, there is the true void.

Until one knows the true Way, one takes oneself to be on a sound path and considers one's own views good, whether one looks through the Buddhist teaching or through common worldly principles. But when these are measured against the great standards of the world with a straight heart, each person's partiality and each person's distortion lead them away from the true Way. Knowing this, take straightforwardness as the root and the true mind as the Way. Practise strategy broadly, correctly, and openly. Grasp the large perspective, adopt emptiness as the path, and regard the path as emptiness.

Emptiness holds good without evil. Wisdom is present, benefit is present, the Way is present, and the heart is empty. Set down on the 12th day of the 5th month in Shōhō year two (1645) by Shinmen Musashi, addressed to Terao Magonojo. Dated the 5th day of the 2nd month in Kanbun year seven (1667), with the monogram of Terao Musei Katsunobu, addressed to Yamamoto Gensuke.
sections.gist: The void is not ignorance but a clear mind that comes after long training, seeing things straight and without clouds.
sections.lesson: Not knowing something is not emptiness. Real calm comes from disciplined practice and an open mind that sees a situation clearly before acting.
